default.description: The trusted cockpit WEBVIEW, and only it, may bind the frame stream, submit human-control intents, acknowledge frames, take interaction holds, and open or dismiss the terminal surface. D.1.3c·2c·1b·1 added allow-terminal-surface here rather than to terminal.json: the pane that RENDERS a terminal must not be the thing that decides one exists, and the command takes a boolean — no label, no URL — so it cannot be aimed at a webview of the caller's choosing. It is granted no core permission at all: the frame stream is a Channel the frontend constructs and hands over, so nothing here needs the event system — and core:default, which W.2 granted, carries core:event:default, whose emit and emit-to are the ability to inject into the application's own event bus. W.2.1 said `windows` here, which grants every webview inside that window: tauri's resolver is an OR over the two lists (`ipc/authority.rs`, resolve_access), so a pane hosted INSIDE the cockpit window would have inherited all of this. A browser or application pane is going to be exactly that, so the grant is to the webview label and the window list is empty.

terminal.description: D.1.3c·2c·1b — the terminal pane WEBVIEW, and only it, may offer a byte sink, acknowledge consumed output, and close the presentation. It holds no `intent`, so it cannot submit a mutation; no `bind_frame_stream`, so it cannot become a second reader of the world; and no core permission, so it cannot reach the application's event bus. The three it does hold are the read-only terminal surface and there is no fourth: terminal input and terminal resize have no command in this process, which is what makes OBSERVE a scope rather than a stage. `webviews` and not `windows` for the reason default.json states — tauri's resolver is an OR over the two lists, so a window grant reaches every webview inside that window, and this pane lives inside the cockpit's own window.
